text:
A: Hello. Can you hear me?
B: Yeah, hiya. Loud and clear. I'm Callum.
A: Callum. That's my son's name, funnily enough. I'm Karen.
B: Oh right, good name then. How old's he?
A: Twenty. Second year at university in Leeds. He hasn't rung me in a week, so I've been moaning about him to strangers all afternoon.
B: Ha. I'll try not to take it personally.
A: Don't. Where are you, then?
B: Long Eaton. Between Nottingham and Derby. You?
A: Stourbridge. Black Country. And before you ask, it's not Birmingham.
B: I wasn't going to say it. I'd have got it wrong, mind.
A: Most people do. So what do you do?
B: I'm a joiner. Small heritage firm in Beeston: sash windows, doors, staircases, mostly old houses and a few listed ones. I'm leading hand, so I've got a two-man fitting crew. At the minute we're doing a Georgian townhouse in Southwell, all the original windows. You're saving as much of the old timber as you can, splicing new wood in where it's rotten, and it's got to match so you can't see the join, you know what I mean?
A: I do, actually. I manage repairs for a housing association. Three supervisors, about forty operatives and contractors.
B: Oh, right. So you're the client, sort of.
A: I'm the one who rings you at half seven asking why you haven't turned up.
B: Ha. Fair. I'd like to think I'd be there.
A: You look like you would. You've tidied up for the camera, which is more than some of mine do. Although you've got sawdust on your collar.
B: Have I? Er, yeah, I've come straight from the workshop. Sorry.
A: Don't apologise, it's honest. My husband's an electrician. He comes in looking like he's been dragged through a loft.
B: Is he self-employed?
A: He is. Which means he leaves his van across our drive and calls it an office.
B: Ha. My dad's the same with his garage, except it's my offcuts in there, so I can't really talk.
A: Do you not have your own place?
B: Er, no. I'm back at my mum and dad's at the minute. Saving for a deposit. Twenty-eight and living at home, I know.
A: Oh, give over. That's sensible. I'd have my two back tomorrow if it meant they had a house at the end of it. Do you pay your mum rent?
B: I do, yeah. And I cook a couple of nights and do all the DIY, so I think I'm worth it.
A: You're a better bargain than mine, then. Do you do much on the housing side? Council houses, that sort of thing?
B: Not really. Most social housing's uPVC now, isn't it. We're mostly private, people with period houses who want the original stuff kept.
A: It is, and half of that's going on me now. Fifteen-year-old units with the hinges dropping. Head office bought them cheap and I'm the one picking up the bill.
B: That's the thing with timber, though. Look after it and it'll outlast us both. Some of those Southwell frames are two hundred years old.
A: Don't tell my finance director, he'll want them in all the flats.
B: Ha. I'd take the work.
A: So what's your lunch on a job like that, then? You lot always seem to live on bacon baps.
B: Baps? It's a cob, round here.
A: It's a bap. I'll not be moved on that.
B: I'll give you that one, then. Cob with chips from the bakery near the workshop, usually. Not the healthiest.
A: I've been told to cut down on salt, so don't tell me about chips. I'm still having my bacon bap on a Saturday, mind.
B: Sounds like the right priorities. Do you get out much, walking or anything?
A: Clent Hills with the dog most weekends. Biscuit, Border terrier, getting on a bit. My knee's not much better than his.
